lines: This church in Venice stands on about a million tree trunks. And so does almost every building around it.
Venice sits on more than a hundred islands of soft mud in a lagoon. Put a heavy stone building on that, and it starts to sink.
Step one: drive wooden piles. Trunks of larch, oak and alder, up to three and a half meters long, about nine in every square meter.
Workers called battipali hammered them in by hand, singing to keep the rhythm. They started at the outer edge and spiraled in toward the center.
Step two: saw the tops off level, below the waterline, and lay a platform of thick wooden planks across them.
Step three: a base of Istrian stone. It soaks up almost no water, so salt from the lagoon can't creep up into the brick walls above.
So why doesn't the wood rot? Down in the mud there's almost no oxygen, so fungi and insects can't attack it. Only slow bacteria do, and water fills the gaps, so the piles keep their shape.
A hundred and twenty one islands. Four hundred and thirty five bridges. All standing on an upside down forest, for centuries.
